name: Palermo Cathedral
label: Palermo Cathedral
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Piazza Sett'Angeli' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Piazza Sett'Angeli' (way/404575624): middle (53 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/49750033: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Palermo Cathedral' (138 m across).
notes: Norman-Arab-Baroque cathedral with a striking facade.

text.description: Palermo Cathedral is a building that has been changed many times, and that is what makes it fun to photograph. The first church on the site was Byzantine, and the present one was begun in 1185 by Archbishop Walter Ophamil. The towers gained their upper levels in the 14th and 15th centuries. The Gothic-Catalan south porch dates from around 1465. The large dome and the neoclassical look come from work done between 1781 and 1801. From here you see the three apses, with their blind arches and geometric patterns that echo Monreale Cathedral. One guide describes this as the cathedral's most original part, and it is usually quieter than the front. The apse area belongs to the original 12th-century building, so you are looking at the oldest outside walls. Stand back, keep the verticals straight with the gridlines, and fill the frame with the pattern work. If you want the full facade as well, Piazza della Cattedrale shows the whole front with the domes and towers. Corso Vittorio Emanuele gives a view of the cathedral framed through the arch gate along the street.
text.geographic_location: The cathedral stands in the old centre of Palermo, next to the Archbishop's Palace (now the Museo Diocesano). Corso Vittorio Emanuele gives a view of it through the arch gate.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from the old centre of Palermo near Corso Vittorio Emanuele, or come by taxi or hired scooter and ask for the cathedral (the Cattedrale). Walk round to Piazza della Cattedrale if you want the main front and south porch. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole rear of the building. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the square is too tight to fit all three apses. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for close-ups of the blind arches and patterns.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Piazza Sett'Angeli (rear of the cathedral, looking at the three apses). The rear of the building with its three apses and the blind-arch and geometric patterns that echo Monreale Cathedral. From here you look straight at the three apses and their blind-arch and geometric decoration, which echoes Monreale Cathedral.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the apses up with the vertical lines so the walls do not lean. Take one wide shot of all three apses, then a closer telephoto shot of the patterned stonework. For the full facade and domes, walk to Piazza della Cattedrale. Corso Vittorio Emanuele gives a street view through the arch gate.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stonework to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the pale sky does not wash out the detail. If you use ultra-wide, keep the phone level to avoid stretched edges.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Light in the morning is likely to suit the apses best. Early in the day is also quieter. Check the light on the day, as high walls can throw shade across the square.

text.access_note: Piazza Sett'Angeli is an open public square. Entry to the cathedral is free, but the roof, royal tombs and treasury need a ticket, and opening hours change with services, so check the official site before you go.

name: Teatro Massimo
label: Teatro Massimo
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Piazza Giuseppe Verdi' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Piazza Giuseppe Verdi' (relation/6683319): middle (315 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/24937131: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Teatro Massimo Vittorio Emanuele' (158 m across).
notes: Italy's largest opera house, famous for its steps.

text.description:
Teatro Massimo is Palermo's grand opera house, and its front is made for a phone photo. A broad flight of steps leads up to a neoclassical facade of tall columns, with a big bronze group and a lion on each side. The architect, Giovan Battista Filippo Basile, took ideas from the Greek temples at Selinunte and Agrigento, and you can see that temple look in the portico. It is the largest theatre in Italy, and it was one of the biggest in Europe when it opened on 16 May 1897 with Verdi's Falstaff. Building began in 1874 and stopped for eight years along the way. The theatre later closed for repairs in 1974 and stayed shut until 1997. Film fans may know it from the closing scenes of The Godfather Part III.

The building is large and symmetrical, so the main job is to fit it all in. The open square in front gives you room to step back, and a few people or café tables in the foreground add a sense of scale. Once you have the full front, move closer and use zoom for the bronze lions, the sculpted groups and the column tops. Tour groups tend to gather on the main steps, so photograph the steps from the square rather than standing on them. For a quieter, more symmetrical view of the columns and statues, try the narrow Via Bara all'Olivella as an alternative.
text.geographic_location: Teatro Massimo stands on Piazza Verdi in Palermo, Sicily, and the square is the open space in front of the theatre's main steps.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for Piazza Verdi in Palermo on foot or by local transport. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to get the whole facade and its columns in one frame. If the square is busy or the edges look stretched, switch to the default lens (1x) and step back. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the bronze lions and column details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Piazza Giuseppe Verdi (centre of the square, facing the front facade). The full neoclassical front of the theatre with its column details, framed by the square and any pedestrians or café tables in front. Face the front of the theatre, which lies to the south-east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line a column or the central doorway up with the middle grid line so the building looks balanced. Keep the phone level and avoid tilting it upwards, or the columns will lean inwards. Leave a little square in the foreground. For a different take, try the quieter, symmetrical view down Via Bara all'Olivella.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the facade to focus, then slide the exposure down a touch if the sky is bright, so the stonework keeps its detail. Take a few frames while people cross the square and pick the one with the best spacing.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: About 45 minutes before sunset is suggested for the front. Sunset time changes with the season, so check the local time on the day.

text.access_note: The facade and square are an open public space, but the interior, including the auditorium, is open only on paid guided tours, so check the official site before you go.

name: Catacombe dei Cappuccini
label: Capuchin Catacombs
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from the Wikipedia article 'Catacombe dei Cappuccini'.
notes: Famous catacombs with mummified bodies.

text.description:
The Capuchin Catacombs are burial galleries beneath the Capuchin monastery in Palermo. The monks began digging crypts here in the 16th century, when their original cemetery ran out of room. In 1599 they mummified Brother Silvestro of Gubbio, a recently deceased friar, and placed him in the catacombs. Over the following centuries local families paid to have their relatives preserved here too, and the halls are arranged by group: men, women, children, priests, monks and professionals. The catacombs hold about 8,000 bodies, including 1,252 mummies counted in a 2011 census.

This is an unusual place to photograph, and the most important thing to know is that photography inside is officially prohibited. Prominent signs say so, and iron grilles keep visitors away from the bodies. Please respect that. The people here were real, and they include children. Treat the inside as somewhere to look and learn rather than to take pictures.

What you can do is take a record of the visit from outside: the approach, the monastery frontage and the entrance area, which help you remember the day. Keep the phone away once you go through the door, and follow any instructions from the staff. If you want to know more about the people buried here, the history is well documented, including a scientific study of the mummies that began in 2007. Opening times and entry rules can change, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: In Palermo, Sicily, underneath the city's Capuchin monastery.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stops are listed for this spot, so start from the centre of Palermo and go by taxi or hired scooter to the Capuchin monastery. The phone icon on the map marks the place, so you can follow it on your phone as you arrive. Check the official site for entry arrangements before you go. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Outside only: use the default lens (1x) for the entrance and frontage. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close to the building and want it all in the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Stay outside the building to take your photos, and step back a little so the whole frontage fits in.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the building's vertical lines straight. Include a little of the surroundings to show where you are. Photograph the exterior only, and keep other visitors out of shot where you can.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the building to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the walls don't wash out. Switch the phone to silent and keep it away inside, where photography is prohibited.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daytime, when the outside light is clear and the entrance is easy to see. Earlier in the day is likely to be quieter.

text.access_note: The catacombs are open to the public, but photography inside is officially prohibited; check the official site before you go for entry details and current rules.

name: Ballarò
label: Ballarò Market
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Via Porta Carini' (1 web pages); placed at the stretch of Via Porta Carini nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OSM N3450499385 (Ballarò): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Historic street market in Albergheria.

text.description: Ballarò is one of Palermo's busy street markets, and it photographs best as a scene of people and food rather than a single building. It suits the early start: stallholders arrange colourful produce into displays as the stalls open, and the crowds have not yet arrived. That gives you clear colour, tidy stacks of fruit and vegetables, and room to frame a shot without people filling the foreground. Later in the day the streets fill with shoppers, which makes a different picture: on Via Ballarò, stalls and people are packed together, with the dome of the Chiesa del Carmine Maggiore rising behind the crowd. Fish stalls with whole swordfish and tuna laid out on the counters are also worth a look along the market street. Keep your phone ready but your manner relaxed. Ask before photographing vendors or people up close, since a smile and a gesture usually does it. Some vendors may ask for a small payment, so decide beforehand how you will handle that. Stalls change from day to day, so treat any list of what you will see as a guide, not a promise. Keep your bag zipped and your phone in your hand or on a wrist strap while you walk through the crowd.
text.geographic_location: Its stalls run along Via Ballarò, with the dome of the Chiesa del Carmine Maggiore rising behind the crowd.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stops are listed for this spot. From there the Ballarò stalls on Via Ballarò lie about 900 m to the south-east. On Via Ballarò, the dome of the Chiesa del Carmine Maggiore rises behind the crowd. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for stalls and displays; it is the lens the camera app opens with. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) in the narrowest parts to fit in a whole stall front. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out details, or to photograph people from a polite distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Via Porta Carini (the market entrance from Via Porta Carini). Vendors arranging colorful produce into displays as the stalls open. Stay to the side so you do not block the way in or out of the market.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Shoot along the line of stalls so the colours stack up in rows, and turn on gridlines to keep the stall edges straight. Fill the frame with one display rather than the whole street. If you walk on to Via Ballarò, try one wider shot of stalls and shoppers with the dome of the Chiesa del Carmine Maggiore behind them.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap to focus on the produce, then slide the exposure down a little so the bright colours do not wash out. Use portrait mode for a close shot of a single stall item, and ask permission before you photograph a vendor.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Around 8 AM, when vendors arrange their produce; one guide suggests 8-9 AM, so treat the timing as approximate.

text.access_note: This is a street market in public streets, but stalls and trading times vary, so check the stalls on the day and ask before photographing vendors.
claims_not_in_sources: Early morning crowds are smaller than later in the day.
Stalls and what they sell change from day to day.
Pickpocketing can be a risk in busy market crowds, so keep bags zipped.

name: Quattro Canti
label: Quattro Canti
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Teatro Massimo' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Teatro Massimo Vittorio Emanuele' (way/24937131): middle (158 m across); moved 35 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/426480998: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Quattro Canti' (41 m across).
notes: Baroque crossroads with four curved facades.

text.description:
Quattro Canti, officially Piazza Vigliena, is the Baroque crossroads at the heart of old Palermo, where Via Maqueda meets Corso Vittorio Emanuele (the Cassaro). It was laid out between 1608 and 1620 on the orders of the Spanish Viceroys. The square is octagonal. Four sides are streets, and the other four are matching concave facades, each four storeys high. Each facade has a fountain for one of the seasons at the bottom, statues of Spanish rulers of Sicily above that, and statues of four female patron saints of Palermo at the top. That repeated, curved design is what makes it so rewarding to photograph.

From here you look down Via Maqueda towards the Quattro Canti at the far end of the street. It is a calmer way to photograph the crossing than standing in the middle of it, though the square will look small in your frame. Use the telephoto lens to bring it closer and keep the street lines straight. For the full octagon with all four facades, walk down to Piazza Vigliena itself and use the ultra-wide lens (0.5x). The square is busy around midday, so early morning or evening is easier.
text.geographic_location: Quattro Canti sits in the centre of Palermo's historic quarter, where Via Maqueda crosses Corso Vittorio Emanuele. The church of San Giuseppe dei Padri Teatini stands on one corner, and Piazza Pretoria is a few steps away.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot; head to Teatro Massimo and go up to the top of its steps. From there the Quattro Canti is about 655 m to the south-east, down Via Maqueda. Walk down Via Maqueda to reach the crossing itself. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: From the Teatro Massimo steps, use the telephoto lens (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring the far end of Via Maqueda closer. At the square itself, switch to the ultra-wide lens (0.5x) to fit the whole octagon in. The default lens (1x) suits one facade at a time.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Teatro Massimo (top of the steps of the opera house, facing Piazza Giuseppe Verdi). A distant view down Via Maqueda, with the Quattro Canti visible at the far end of the street, best taken with a zoom lens. The Quattro Canti is at the far end of the street, so it will be small in the frame. For a closer view, walk to Piazza Vigliena. Stand in the middle of the crossing for all four facades with their fountains and statues, or face one facade straight on rather than at a sharp angle, to show a complete concave palace front.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: From the steps, use gridlines to keep the street edges straight and let Via Maqueda lead the eye to the buildings at the end. People and traffic will be in the way, so take a few frames. Down in the square, tilt the phone as little as you can, so the facades do not lean inwards. A straight-on shot of one facade shows the fountain, the statues and the rooflines in one frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the buildings at the far end of the street to focus, then lower the exposure slider slightly if the sky is bright. Take a few shots in a row, because pedestrians and vehicles keep moving through the view.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or evening, as the square is busy at midday.

text.access_note: The Quattro Canti is an open public square, but check locally for any closures or restrictions before you go, especially if you plan to use a tripod.

name: Cappella Palatina
label: Palatine Chapel
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/400424488: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Palatine Chapel' (39 m across).
notes: Golden Byzantine mosaics inside the Norman Palace.

text.description:
The Cappella Palatina is the royal chapel of the Norman Palace in Palermo, and it is a small, richly decorated space that rewards a slow look. King Roger II commissioned it in 1132, building over an older chapel from around 1080 that is now the crypt. The design blends Byzantine, Norman and Fatimid styles, a reminder of how mixed Sicily was in the 12th century. It was recognised by UNESCO in 2015 as part of the Arab-Norman Palermo group of sites.

For photographs there are three things to look for. The first is the gold-and-colour mosaics on the walls, dome and transept, with figures of saints and gardens of plants and animals. The second is the carved wooden muqarnas ceiling over the nave, a honeycomb-like ceiling that is the earliest surviving wooden example of its kind. It carries painted scenes of musicians, hunters and animals, and about 75 inscriptions. The third is the rhythm of six pointed arches on old classical columns, which leads the eye towards the three apses.

On a phone, think in layers: one wide shot to show the whole nave, then closer shots of the details. Interiors like this are dim and the gold is shiny, so tap on a bright mosaic and lower the exposure slider a little to keep the colours rich. Hold your phone steady and breathe out as you press the shutter. Check the chapel's rules on photography before you go.
text.geographic_location: The chapel is the royal chapel of the Norman Palace in Palermo, Sicily.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot. The chapel is in the Norman Palace in Palermo. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the whole nave and ceiling, then switch to the default lens (1x) for walls and arches. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out mosaic figures and the muqarnas ceiling.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From there you are at the centre of the chapel, with the arches, the ceiling and the mosaics around you.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the rows of arches with the vertical lines so the nave looks straight. Tilt the phone up a little for the ceiling, and keep a steady, level hold so the lines don't lean. For mosaics, step in close, keep the phone parallel to the wall and fill the frame with one scene or figure.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on a bright patch of gold mosaic to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the gold does not burn out. Night mode can help in the dim corners, but hold very still while it works. Avoid flash, which bounces off the shiny mosaic. Check the official site before you go for any rules on photography.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a time when the chapel is open and not too crowded, so you can stand still and get a clean view down the nave.

text.access_note: This is a historic royal chapel inside the Norman Palace, so check the official site before you go for access and any rules.

name: Palazzo dei Normanni
label: Norman Palace
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Piazza del Parlamento' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Piazza del Parlamento' (way/740441916): middle (301 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/395010: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Palazzo dei Normanni' (252 m across).
notes: Royal palace of the Norman kings.

text.description:
The Palazzo dei Normanni, also called the Royal Palace, is a long, pale limestone building on the highest ground in Palermo. It is often described as the oldest royal residence in Europe. The Normans built a new castle-palace there after the conquest of 1072, on the site of an earlier Arab-period fortress. Later rulers added courtyards, including the Fountain Courtyard in 1584 and the Maqueda Courtyard in 1600. Since 1946 it has housed the Sicilian Regional Assembly, so it is still a working building. Inside is the Cappella Palatina, begun after Roger II's coronation in 1130, famous for its mosaics and painted wooden roof.

The viewpoint is Piazza del Parlamento, in front of the main façade, where you face the front of the palace straight on. From the square, the plain white façade, the pointed-arch windows and the arcaded loggia all sit in one wide, calm picture. The building is long, so the main job is fitting it in. Stand back, keep the phone level, and let the square give you some empty foreground. Once you have the full-width shot, step closer and pick out single details, such as one run of arches or a pair of windows. For a different view, the palace gardens frame the walls and towers with palm trees, and Via del Bastione looks up at the palace from the street.
text.geographic_location: The palace stands on the highest ground in Palermo. Its main façade faces Piazza del Parlamento, and its guide address is Piazza Indipendenza 1.
text.directions_text: No Underground, station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so navigate by map to Piazza del Parlamento, in front of the palace, or to Piazza Indipendenza 1. If you are unsure of the entrance, use Piazza Indipendenza 1 as the palace address. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole long façade in from the square. Then switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural look. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the pointed windows and the arcaded loggia.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Piazza del Parlamento (in front of the main façade). The palace's austere white limestone main façade with its pointed-arch windows and arcaded loggia, seen straight on from the square.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and line the horizontal rows of arches and windows up with them, holding the phone level so the walls do not lean. Leave some open square at the bottom of the picture to give the building room. If you want a second view, try the palace gardens, where the walls and towers sit behind palm and other trees, or Via del Bastione for the lit façade in the evening.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the pale façade to focus. Then drag the exposure slider down a little so the limestone keeps its detail and the sky is not washed out. Use panorama only if the ultra-wide still cuts off the ends, and move slowly.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Softer morning or late-afternoon light usually suits pale stone better than harsh midday sun. In the evening, Via del Bastione is recommended for the lit façade and its golden mosaics against the sky.

text.access_note: The square in front of the palace is open public space, but the palace is a working parliament building, so check the official site before you go for the interior, gardens and terraces.

name: Fontana Pretoria
label: Pretoria Fountain
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Palazzo Pretorio' (2 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Genio di Palazzo Pretorio' (pois); moved 5 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/926546483: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Pretoria Fountain' (34 m across).
notes: Monumental Renaissance fountain.

text.description: Fontana Pretoria is a huge, tiered fountain that fills most of Piazza Pretoria in Palermo's historic centre. Statues of the twelve Olympian gods, other mythological figures, animals and the rivers of Palermo are packed around its basins, so it rewards both wide shots and close ones. It was made in Florence in the sixteenth century by Francesco Camilliani, then bought by Palermo and taken apart into 644 pieces. It arrived on 26 May 1574 and was rebuilt in the square, with Camillo Camilliani finishing the work in 1581. Some statues were damaged on the way, and others may have been kept back by the previous owner. The nude figures and the city's reputation at the time led to the nickname "Piazza della Vergogna" (Square of Shame). A restoration ran from 1998 to 2003. The fountain is hard to fit into one frame from ground level, because the square gives you little room to step back. The best full view is from the steps of Palazzo Pretorio, looking across the fountain towards Via Maqueda. From there the basins and statues sit in the foreground, with the square and its buildings behind. Come back afterwards for close-ups of the carved figures and reliefs, and for low upward angles that show how tall the fountain is. The fountain has a fenced perimeter, and renovation work has been reported, so check that your viewpoint is not blocked.
text.geographic_location: In Piazza Pretoria, in the historic centre of Palermo, on the west side of the church of Santa Caterina and one block south of the Quattro Canti crossroads.
text.directions_text: Head for the Quattro Canti crossroads in the historic centre, then walk one block south to Piazza Pretoria. If you are coming from further out, head to the Quattro Canti area and finish on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to get the whole fountain in one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a tidier view, and to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for faces, reliefs and niches.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Palazzo Pretorio (steps of the building, looking across the fountain toward Via Maqueda). The whole fountain in one frame, with the tiered basins and statues in the foreground and the surrounding square and buildings behind. The fountain lies to the north-west of you. The steps may be restricted, so use them only if allowed.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the verticals straight so the tiers do not lean. Put the fountain in the lower half and let the buildings fill the background. For a different view, try Piazza Pretoria itself to show the buildings framing the fountain. Close to the fenced edge, shoot upwards with the telephoto lens for detail and height.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stonework to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the pale stone looks washed out. After dark, use night mode and rest your elbows on something steady. A Live Photo can help if people walk through your frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning is quieter, and late afternoon gives a warmer glow. After dark the fountain is lit from below, which makes good night shots.

text.access_note: Piazza Pretoria surrounds a fountain with a fenced perimeter, and the Palazzo Pretorio steps may be restricted, so check on the spot whether access is allowed.
claims_not_in_sources: Pale stone can look washed out in bright light, so lowering exposure may help.
The ultra-wide lens (0.5x) helps fit the whole fountain in when there is little room to step back.

name: La Vucciria market
label: Vucciria Market
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Piazza Caracciolo' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Piazza Caracciolo' (node/8987672182): point.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/442940353: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'La Vucciria' (129 m across).
notes: Historic market and nightlife area.

text.description:
La Vucciria is one of Palermo's old market districts, a tangle of pedestrian alleys and small squares in the Castellammare quarter. It is usually described as running from the church and square of San Domenico in the north down to Via Vittorio Emanuele in the south, with Via Roma along its western side. Its look is busy and a little rough around the edges: weathered buildings, graffiti, hand-painted signs, and traders calling out their wares. The name is a puzzle. Some say it comes from 'voce' (voice), for the noise of the sellers, others from the French 'boucherie' (butcher's shop).

It photographs well because everything happens at street level and close together. Piazza Caracciolo, at the south end where the market finishes, is the best place to start. Fishmongers cut fish on trestle tables in the open, and nearby stalls sell produce and fabric. Work in layers: a wide shot of the whole scene, then a closer shot of a table, a pile of fruit or a hanging sign. Just off Via Argenteria, in a small square in front of the ruined church of Sant'Eulalia dei Catalani, there is also one of the oldest carved images of the Genius of Palermo in the city, which makes a quiet detail shot. Mornings are the liveliest time, but opening times seem to vary, so check locally before you set out early.
text.geographic_location: In the old Castellammare quarter of central Palermo, between San Domenico church to the north, Via Roma to the west and Via Vittorio Emanuele to the south.
text.directions_text: There are no tram or railway stops at this spot, so the market is reached on foot through the old town. Head for Via Vittorio Emanuele, the southern edge of the market, and walk north into the alleys to reach Piazza Caracciolo. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the scene as your eye sees it. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) when the alleys feel too tight. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out fish tables and stall details from a polite distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Piazza Caracciolo (south end, where the market finishes). Fishmongers cutting fish on trestle tables and stalls with produce and fabrics, framed by the square's street life.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put a fish table on one of the lower lines, with the stalls and people filling the upper part of the frame. Then step in for a closer shot of one stall. If you have time, Piazza Garraffello is a good second viewpoint, with its weathered Baroque palaces, old loggia and street-art on the facades behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the busiest table to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky or bright wall behind it is washing out. Try portrait mode on stall details such as fruit or fish on ice, and a Live Photo to catch the movement of the sellers. Ask before taking close portraits of people.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning, roughly 8 to 10 a.m., when the square is partly shaded and the light is softer than at midday. Check locally first, as stall hours vary.

text.access_note: An open public market area of streets and squares; there is no entrance ticket, but check locally for stall times before you go.

name: Teatro Politeama
label: Teatro Politeama
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Piazza Ruggero Settimo' (5 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Piazza Ruggero Settimo' (way/740441919): middle (168 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/30877778: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Politeama Garibaldi' (110 m across).
notes: Neoclassical theatre with a bronze chariot on the arch.

text.description: The Politeama is the grand neoclassical theatre in the middle of Palermo's central square, and it is easy to photograph because the whole front is built to be seen head-on. A triumphal-arch entrance is topped by a bronze quadriga, a four-horse chariot group by Mario Rutelli showing the Triumph of Apollo and Euterpe. A curved double row of columns wraps around the entrance. The theatre opened on 7 June 1874 with Bellini's I Capuleti e i Montecchi, and it took its Garibaldi name after his death in 1882. Today it is the second most important theatre in the city after the Teatro Massimo, and it is the home of the Orchestra Sinfonica Siciliana. From Piazza Ruggero Settimo you get the classic frontal view. The monument to Ruggero Settimo stands in the foreground, and a palm tree nearby gives a natural frame. Put the monument low in the picture and let the arch and the quadriga fill the upper part. The square is big, so a phone's ultra-wide lens helps if you want the whole front plus some sky. Viale della Libertà is another place to see the theatre, but check the exact angle on the day. Try a few steps left and right to keep passers-by out of the way of the monument.
text.geographic_location: In central Palermo, in Piazza Ruggero Settimo, at the start of Viale della Libertà. The theatre is in the square.
text.directions_text: No public transport stop is listed for this spot, so head for the central Piazza Ruggero Settimo in Palermo. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the classic frontal view. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the monument, the whole facade and some sky together, and to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the quadriga and the arch details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Piazza Ruggero Settimo (frontal view from the square, with the Ruggero Settimo monument in the foreground). The neoclassical facade with its triumphal-arch entrance and bronze quadriga, framed by the monument to Ruggero Settimo standing in front of the theatre.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Use the monument and the palm tree as foreground, and turn on gridlines to keep the facade straight. Place the arch near the centre, with the quadriga on the upper line of the grid.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the facade to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky stays blue and the lit stonework is not washed out. After dark, use night mode and rest your elbows against a railing or wall to keep the picture sharp.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: After dark, when the building is lit and the square looks especially striking. Daytime also works, but expect more people in the foreground.

text.access_note: The square is an open public space; for performances or going inside the theatre, check the official site before you go.

name: Piazza Marina
label: Piazza Marina
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Giardino Garibaldi' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Giardino Garibaldi' (way/24891138): middle (196 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/739764754: 'Fontana del Garraffo', the best-known feature inside 'Piazza Marina' (351 m across).
notes: Large square with Giardino Garibaldi's giant ficus trees.

text.description:
Piazza Marina is a large square in the Kalsa quarter, in the historic centre of Palermo, and the Garibaldi Garden fills much of its middle. The garden is the best reason to bring your phone out here. It was designed by Giovan Battista Filippo Basile in 1863 and is known for the biggest Ficus macrophylla in Europe. The huge trunks and hanging aerial roots make strong, graphic pictures. Around the square you also get a mix of palaces, churches and the Fontana del Garraffo, so there is plenty to turn towards once you have your tree shots.

The square has a long history. In the Middle Ages this was a swamp linked to the old port, the Cala, and it was cleared in the 14th century. Later the Inquisition used the space for its convictions. In 1909 the New York police officer Joe Petrosino was killed here, and a small brass memorial plate on a pole recalls him.

For photos, start beneath the biggest fig trees, near the turtle pond, and look up and along the roots. Then walk to the square's edge for the colourful façades with wrought-iron balconies and lamp posts. The Sunday flea market makes the square crowded, so choose another day if you want clear frames.
text.geographic_location: In the Kalsa quarter of Palermo's historic centre, at the foot of Cassaro street. The Garibaldi Garden sits in the middle of the square.
text.directions_text: Head for the Kalsa quarter at the foot of Cassaro street. Once you reach the square, walk into the Garibaldi Garden and find the biggest fig trees by the turtle pond. From there the Fontana del Garraffo is to the west, about 2 minutes on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the fig trunks and aerial roots, and the default lens (1x) for the square's façades and the fountain. If your phone has a telephoto (2x-5x), use it for details such as balconies and lamp posts.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Giardino Garibaldi (beneath the largest fig trees, around the turtle pond). The huge ficus trees with their aerial roots, with the garden's greenery and the square's edge behind them. The Fontana del Garraffo lies to the west of this point.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place a thick trunk on one vertical line, letting the roots hang through the frame. Crouch low and tilt the phone up for height. For an alternative, step out to Piazza Marina itself and frame the colourful façades, wrought-iron balconies and lamp posts. The church of Santa Maria della Catena is also nearby, but check that it is open before relying on it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on a bright patch of leaves to set focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the bright sky does not wash out the greens. If a Live Photo is on, hold still for a moment after pressing the button.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when the light is softer. The tree shade also helps at midday.

text.access_note: The Sunday flea market makes the square crowded.

name: Church of Santa Maria dell'Ammiraglio
label: La Martorana
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Piazza Bellini' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Piazza Bellini' (way/442849021): middle (111 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/86870886: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Church of Santa Maria dell’Ammiraglio' (46 m across).
notes: Byzantine mosaics on Piazza Bellini.

text.description:
Santa Maria dell'Ammiraglio, also called La Martorana, is one of Palermo's most layered churches, and Piazza Bellini gives you the easiest outdoor view of it. From the square you see the Baroque facade and bell tower, with the red domes of the neighbouring San Cataldo church just beside them. Both churches fit into one frame, which is why this is the classic picture of the pair.

The church was founded by George of Antioch, the admiral and chief minister of King Roger II of Sicily, which is where the name comes from. Its foundation charter dates to 1143, and it was complete by George's death in 1151. Later, nuns from a neighbouring convent altered it between the 16th and 18th centuries, so Byzantine, Norman and Baroque styles now sit together. The nuns were also known for their fruit-shaped marzipan, still sold in Palermo pastry shops. Since 2015 the church has been part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site Arab-Norman Palermo and the Cathedral Churches of Cefalù and Monreale.

For a phone photo, stand back in the square so the whole facade fits without tilting the phone upwards. Switch on the gridlines and keep the vertical lines of the bell tower parallel to the edges of the screen. Then move closer, or use zoom, for a second shot of the details. The interior has gold mosaics, but you need to go inside to see them, and photography rules may differ, so look for signs.
text.geographic_location: In the historic centre of Palermo, on Piazza Bellini. The church overlooks the square, next to the Norman church of San Cataldo and facing the Baroque church of Santa Caterina.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stop is listed for this spot, so the simplest way to reach it is by taxi or hired scooter, asking for Piazza Bellini in the old centre of Palermo. Once you are in the square, the church is on its edge, with San Cataldo's red domes next to it. Santa Caterina stands on the opposite side. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the facade and the domes together. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the square is busy and you cannot step back far enough. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the bell tower and the red domes of San Cataldo.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Piazza Bellini (across the square from the church facade). The Baroque facade and bell tower of the church, with the neighbouring San Cataldo church's red domes beside it. Face south-east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the bell tower with a vertical line. Keep the phone level, so the buildings do not lean. Leave a little paving in the foreground to show the square. If you go inside, the gold mosaics of the nave and dome look best framed symmetrically between the columns.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the church wall to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky does not turn white and the stonework keeps its detail. Take a quick panorama only if the square is quiet, and hold the phone upright as you sweep.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon is usually kinder to the stonework and has fewer people in the square. Check the official site for visiting times if you want to go inside.

text.access_note: The square is an open public space, but the church is a place of worship with modest dress expected and possible entry rules and photography limits, so check the official site before you go.

name: Palazzo Chiaramonte
label: Palazzo Chiaramonte
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Piazza Marina' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Piazza Marina' (way/739764754): middle (350 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/1291721: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Palazzo Chiaramonte-Steri' (64 m across).
notes: Medieval palace on Piazza Marina.

text.description:
Palazzo Chiaramonte, also called Lo Steri, is a fortress-like Gothic palace in the old Kalsa quarter of Palermo. It was begun by 1320 for the powerful Sicilian lord Manfredi III Chiaramonte. Later it housed the Spanish viceroys of Sicily and the Royal Customs, and from 1600 to 1782 it was the seat of the Inquisition's tribunal. Today it is a museum and also holds the rector's offices of the University of Palermo. At the back is the small Gothic church of Sant'Antonio Abate.

It photographs well because the main facade is so strongly patterned. The ground floor is a heavy wall of rough-cut stone. Above it, the upper floor has paired, arched windows, and the roofline is crenellated. The facade looks onto Piazza Marina, and the open space in front gives you room to fit the whole front into one frame without tilting your phone upwards. Piazza Marina is the usual place to take the exterior shot. Stand across the square from the main facade, on the side facing the palace, and the building sits neatly framed by the open space.

Take a wide shot first, then move in on the windows and the top edge. Wait a moment for passers-by to clear the foreground, or keep one in the frame to show the scale of the walls. If you plan to go inside, check the official site before you go, as the palace is a working university building.
text.geographic_location: Palazzo Chiaramonte stands in the Kalsa, the old quarter of Palermo, on Piazza Marina. It faces the Giardino Garibaldi.
text.directions_text: No tram or railway stops are listed close by, so head for the Kalsa quarter and Piazza Marina by taxi or hired scooter. From there the palace is about 2 minutes on foot to the east. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the whole facade. Switch to the telephoto lens (2x or more, depending on your phone) for the windows and the crenellated top. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you are close to the walls, and keep the phone level to avoid leaning lines.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Piazza Marina (standing across the square from the palace's main facade, on the side facing the palace). The palace's fortress-like main facade, with its paired lancet windows and crenellated top, framed by the open square. The palace lies to the east of you.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the vertical edges of the facade with them so the walls look straight. Leave a little of the square in the foreground to give a sense of scale. Then take a closer shot of the windows and roofline with the telephoto lens.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the facade to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the stone keeps its texture. Take a few frames, as passers-by will move through the shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a time when the sun is lower, in the morning or later in the afternoon, so the stonework has soft shadows. Weekday mornings are likely to be quieter.

text.access_note: You can see the facade from the square, but the palace itself is a museum and university building, so check the official site before you go for access and visiting arrangements.

name: Santa Caterina, Palermo
label: Santa Caterina
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Piazza Bellini' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Piazza Bellini' (way/442849021): middle (111 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/49750065: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Chiesa di Santa Caterina' (82 m across).
notes: Baroque church on Piazza Pretoria.

text.description:
Santa Caterina is a Dominican convent church in the old Kalsa quarter of Palermo, right beside the Quattro Canti crossroads. It photographs well because of where it sits. From Piazza Bellini you see its main façade, with the double-ramp staircase and late Renaissance portal. The older churches of the Martorana and San Cataldo stand on the other side of the square and make a natural frame. The result is the classic postcard view of this corner of the city.

The story behind it is simple. A will of 1310 paid for a women's Dominican convent on the site of an admiral's palace. The church was enlarged mainly between 1566 and 1596 and inaugurated on 24 November 1596. Its dome was finished in 1750. The façade is sober and linear, with Corinthian pilasters, so it looks calm against the busier buildings around it.

On your phone, stand back on the square and let the church sit between its neighbours. Keep the phone level, turn on gridlines so the stair ramps and cornice stay straight, and tap the façade to set focus and exposure. A second angle is from Piazza Pretoria, where the church's western side faces the Fontana Pretoria. The fountain may be partly hidden by restoration work, so check on the day. Both squares are public and easy to walk between.
text.geographic_location: In the historic Kalsa quarter of central Palermo, on Piazza Bellini beside the Quattro Canti crossroads. The Martorana and San Cataldo churches stand across the square.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stops are listed for this spot, so head for the Quattro Canti in the historic centre, by taxi or hired scooter if you are coming from further away. Piazza Bellini is just beside it. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the full façade with the neighbouring churches. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you cannot step back far enough. Use telephoto (2x or more) for the portal and the staircase.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Piazza Bellini (stand on the square facing the main façade, with the church's north side in front of you). The church's main façade with its double-ramp staircase and late Renaissance portal, framed by the Martorana and San Cataldo churches across the square.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Place the staircase and portal in the centre and let the neighbouring church fronts fill the edges. Switch on gridlines and line them up with the cornice so the verticals stay straight. For a different view, walk to Piazza Pretoria and photograph the western side with the Fontana Pretoria in front. Check first whether the fountain is under restoration.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the pale stone of the façade to set focus, then lower the exposure slider slightly so the sky stays blue and the detail is not washed out. Keep Live Photos on if you want a spare frame when people walk through.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon is usually calmer and gives softer light on the stonework. Check on the day, as the square can be busy.

text.access_note: The square is an open public space, but the church and former convent are a place of worship and heritage site, so check the official site before you go for visiting arrangements.

name: Zisa, Palermo
label: La Zisa
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Giardino della Zisa' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Giardino della Zisa' (relation/7897700): middle (255 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/186187084: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Castello della Zisa' (47 m across).
notes: Arab-Norman summer palace.

text.description:
The Zisa is a 12th-century Norman summer palace on the western side of Palermo. Work began around 1165 under King William I, using Arab craftsmen, and finished in 1189 under William II. The name comes from an Arabic word meaning 'the Dear one' or 'the Splendid one'. It was part of a much larger royal hunting park, though its gardens have long vanished. In 2015 it was added to the UNESCO Arab-Norman Palermo World Heritage Site.

It photographs well because the main facade is plain, tall and symmetrical, and the garden in front gives you open space to stand back and fit it in. A water axis runs down the middle of the view, which leads the eye towards the entrance. The original design brought water from a pool at the front into the building itself, so the water in your photo echoes the palace's own story. The palace's thick walls and small windows were chosen to keep the inside cool, which gives the exterior its solid, calm look.

From the garden, keep the facade centred and let the water axis and planting frame it in the foreground. For a different feel, Piazza della Zisa shows the palace silhouette with the surrounding neighbourhood and hills behind it. The garden is reported to be open without a ticket, but the palace interior is separate and may be closed at times, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: The Zisa stands in the western part of Palermo, in a residential neighbourhood. The Giardino della Zisa lies directly in front of the palace. Piazza della Zisa is another recommended viewpoint for the palace.
text.directions_text: Head for the western part of Palermo by taxi or hired scooter and ask for the Zisa palace or the Giardino della Zisa. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the whole facade with the garden in front. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close and cannot fit it all in. Use the telephoto/zoom (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the entrance and the upper part of the walls.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Giardino della Zisa (front garden, facing the main facade). The palace's main facade and central water axis framed by the garden in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the water axis on the centre line so the palace sits symmetrically at the end of it. Keep your phone level so the vertical walls do not lean. If you want a second view, Piazza della Zisa shows the palace silhouette against the neighbourhood and hills.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the facade to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the stone keeps its detail. If the water is still, check for reflections before you shoot.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Gentler light, such as morning or late afternoon, usually suits stone facades better than harsh midday sun.

text.access_note: The garden is reported to be open to the public without a ticket, but the palace itself is a separate visit that may be ticketed or closed for restoration, so check the official site before you go.

name: Church of the Gesù, Palermo
label: Chiesa del Gesù
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Piazza Casa Professa' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Piazza Casa Professa' (way/297145894): middle (51 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/332578307: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Chiesa del Gesù (Casa Professa)' (96 m across).
notes: Sumptuous Baroque Jesuit church.

text.description:
The Church of the Gesù, also called Casa Professa, is a Baroque Jesuit church on Piazza Casa Professa in Palermo. The Jesuits arrived in the city in 1549 and began building beside their professed house in the late 16th century. The plan grew grander in the 17th century, when two side naves were added to the central one, and the dome was finished in 1686. The church has a story of loss and recovery too. A bomb brought the dome down in 1943, and after long restoration it reopened on 24 February 2009.

From the square, the façade is the part to photograph. It is split into two levels by a cornice, with three portals below and niches above holding statues of St Ignatius of Loyola, a Madonna with Child and Francis Xavier. The upper level is framed by pilasters and more statues of saints, and the whole thing is topped by a curved gable with the Jesuit emblem. It is quite restrained compared with the richly decorated interior, so it works best as a clean, well-ordered architectural shot rather than a dramatic one.

Stand on the square, take one wide frame to show the whole front in its setting, then move in with zoom for the statues and the portals. Keep your phone upright and level so the tall façade does not lean. If you also plan to go inside, check the official site before you go for access and any photography rules.
text.geographic_location: The church stands at Piazza Casa Professa 21 in Palermo, Sicily. The square lies directly in front of its main façade.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stops are listed for this spot, so head for Piazza Casa Professa in central Palermo by taxi or hired scooter. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the full façade in from the square, then switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural view. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the statues in the niches and the marble portal.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Piazza Casa Professa (in front of the main façade). The Baroque façade of the church across the square, with its stucco statues and marble portal.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line a vertical edge of the façade up with a grid line so the building does not lean. Keep the phone level and held upright. Take one wide shot of the whole front, then a closer one of the portal and statues. If you tilt the phone upward to fit the top, expect the sides to slope inwards, so step back a little instead.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the façade to focus, then slide the exposure down a touch if the sky is bright, so the stonework keeps its detail. Take a few frames at 0.5x, 1x and a zoom level so you can pick the best one later.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Check on the day to see how the light falls on the stonework. Going early in the day is a good option if you want a quieter square.

text.access_note: The church is a place of worship, so dress respectfully if you go inside, and check the official site before you go for visiting times and any photography rules.

name: San Giovanni degli Eremiti
label: San Giovanni Eremiti
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Largo Michele Gerbasi' (1 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Largo San Michele Arcangelo' (roads).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/49786077: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Church of San Giovanni degli Eremiti' (45 m across).
notes: Church with red domes and a cloister garden.

text.description: San Giovanni degli Eremiti is a small former monastery church in the old part of Palermo, and its red domes are the part everyone wants to photograph. The site dates back a very long way. A church and Benedictine monastery stood here before the 6th century, and around 1136, after the Norman conquest, Roger II of Sicily gave it back to Benedictine monks. The domes show the Arab influence that lingered in Sicily when the church was rebuilt in the 12th century. The bright red is not original, though. It was painted in the 19th century during a restoration, after traces of red plaster were found. The cloister next door has slender paired columns, pointed arches, a garden and an old Arab cistern. A guide names this square as a place to see the domes together, so treat it as a distant view rather than a close postcard shot. If you want something closer and more intimate, the church site itself gives a different picture: the small domes rising above the ruined cloister arches, with citrus trees and greenery around them. The inside of the church is almost bare, so the exterior and garden are the main photo subjects. Leave a little empty sky above the domes so they do not feel cramped.
text.geographic_location: In the old Albergaria quarter of Palermo, on Via dei Benedettini, about two blocks south of the Palazzo dei Normanni and next to the church of San Giorgio in Kemonia.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or railway stop is listed for this spot, so start from the Palazzo dei Normanni, which is about two blocks north of the church. A taxi or hired scooter is quicker, so ask for Largo Michele Gerbasi for the viewpoint or Via dei Benedettini for the church itself. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) and leave a little sky above the domes. If the domes look small and distant, move to the telephoto (2x or 3x, depending on your phone) to fill the frame. Inside the cloister garden, the ultra-wide (0.5x) helps in tight spaces, but keep the arches straight so they do not lean.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Largo Michele Gerbasi. The church's five red domes together in one frame, the classic postcard view of the facade. A guide recommends this square for seeing the domes together, so move around the square to find a clear line of sight.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the line of the domes level with a horizontal grid line, with the domes in the upper third and the building beneath them. Tap on a dome to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the red stays rich and the sky does not wash out. For a second, closer picture, shoot from inside the church site, where the small domes rise above the ruined cloister arches and citrus trees.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap to focus on a dome, then drag the exposure slider down slightly. Leave Live Photos on if you like, but the domes are still, so a steady standard shot is usually enough. Skip portrait mode for the exterior, as it can blur the edges of the domes.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light is usually kinder to the red domes than harsh midday sun.

text.access_note: The viewpoint square is an open public space, but the cloister and church site may be ticketed or have set opening times, so check the official site before you go.

name: Church of San Cataldo
label: San Cataldo
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Piazza Bellini' (5 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Piazza Bellini' (way/442849021): middle (111 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/86870896: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Church of San Cataldo' (17 m across).
notes: Small Norman church with three red domes.

text.description: The Church of San Cataldo is a small, compact church from the mid-12th century, built in the Arab-Norman style that is found only in Sicily. It is a plain rectangular block with blind arches along the walls, a bell tower, and three round red domes on the roof. Those domes are the reason people photograph it: the bright red against pale stone and a blue sky makes a strong, simple picture, even on a phone. In the 18th century the building was used as a post office, and it was restored in the 19th century to look closer to its medieval form. It joined the World Heritage list in 2015. Inside, the original mosaic floor and main altar survive, and part of the old city wall runs underneath the church. The classic photo is from Piazza Bellini, looking at the front of the church with the facade and bell tower in view and the red domes above. The neighbouring Martorana church sits beside it and makes a good companion in the frame. Stand back far enough to get the whole building in, then step closer for a tighter shot of the domes. If the square is busy, Piazza della Vittoria gives a wider and quieter angle on the domes with fewer people in the picture. Check what you can see on arrival, as the sightline may differ from what you expect.
text.geographic_location: In central Palermo, on Piazza Bellini, right beside the neighbouring Martorana church.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stop is listed for this spot. The church is on Piazza Bellini in central Palermo. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the facade, bell tower and domes in from close range. Use the default lens (1x) for a more natural look. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the red domes against the sky.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Piazza Bellini (front of the church, facing the facade). The facade and bell tower with the church's red domes, framed beside the neighbouring Martorana church. The church is just to the south of this point.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the bell tower upright so the building does not lean. Include the Martorana church at one edge for context. Then zoom in for a close shot of the domes alone. For a wider, quieter view without people, try Piazza della Vittoria as an alternative.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stonework to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the red domes and the sky keep their colour. Take a few frames from slightly different positions, as the domes look different from each angle.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Golden hour, in the warm light of late afternoon.

text.access_note: This is a place of worship and its opening times may vary, so check the official site before you go.

name: Cuba Palace
label: La Cuba
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Corso Calatafimi' (3 web pages); placed at the stretch of Corso Calatafimi nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/81373199: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Castello della Cuba (Cuba sottana)' (44 m across).
notes: Norman pleasure pavilion.

text.description:
The Cuba is a small royal pleasure palace built in 1180 for William II of Sicily. It stood in the middle of a large royal park, with an artificial lake lapping at its walls, and was meant as a cool place to rest in the heat and hold evening parties. The lake has long gone, which is why the building now looks oddly tall. It is a compact block about 31 by 17 metres, with a tower-like projection in the middle of each side. The outer walls are decorated with pointed arches, and a band of Arabic lettering runs along the top edge. A dome sits over the middle. The name probably comes from its cube shape, or from the Arabic word for dome. Boccaccio even set one of his Decameron tales here.

It photographs well because the shape is so simple and strong: a plain, sandy-coloured block with rows of tall, blind arches. From the street, the front view is the one most visitors take. Corso Calatafimi is a long road, so choose a spot with a clear line of sight to the facade, then step back as far as is safe so the whole building fits. Keep the phone level so the vertical lines stay straight, and use the gridlines to help. Once you have the full view, move in for the arches and the lettering along the cornice. There is also a view from the courtyard, but check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: The Cuba stands on Corso Calatafimi in Palermo. The other small Norman pavilion, the Cubula, is a separate building about half a kilometre to the west.
text.directions_text: Use a map app to reach Corso Calatafimi and the Cuba (Palazzo della Cuba). The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole facade. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the pavement is narrow and you cannot step back far enough. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the arches and the lettering band.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Corso Calatafimi. The palace's front facade, with its large blind pointed arches and the cube-shaped mass of the building, as shown in the front-view photos on Tripadvisor. No exact spot on the street is recommended, so shuffle along the pavement until nothing blocks the facade.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the building's corners with the vertical lines, so the walls do not lean. Leave a little sky above the dome. Try one shot straight on and one from a slight angle to show the depth of the projecting centre. For a different view, the courtyard shows the arcaded walls from inside, but it is ticketed and may be under work.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the pale stonework to focus, then lower the exposure slider a touch so the walls keep their texture and the sky does not turn white. Take care of traffic while you step back from the kerb.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer, warmer light on stone walls. Try to avoid the harshest midday sun, which flattens the arches.

text.access_note: The outside can be seen from the street, but the courtyard and interior are a ticketed site, so check the official site before you go for current access.

name: Oratory of San Lorenzo
label: San Lorenzo Oratory
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/233500615: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Oratorio di San Lorenzo' (23 m across).
notes: Serpotta stuccoes and the Caravaggio Nativity (stolen).

text.description: The Oratory of San Lorenzo is a Baroque prayer hall in the Kalsa quarter, in the historic centre of Palermo. It stands close to the Basilica of Saint Francis of Assisi, so the two are easy to visit on the same walk. The oratory was built in 1569 to replace a smaller church dedicated to St Lawrence. It was paid for by a confraternity of mainly Genoese merchants and was linked to the Conventual Franciscans. Between 1699 and 1706 Giacomo Serpotta added a rich stucco decoration telling the life of St Francis, and this is the main reason to go in with your phone. The oratory is also known for Caravaggio's Nativity with St Francis and St Lawrence, which was stolen in 1969 and never recovered. Since 2015 a hi-tech replica has hung in its place. The stucco figures and the replica altarpiece give you plenty of close detail, and the room itself gives you a sense of scale. Photograph the whole wall first, then move in on a single figure or scene. Rules on photography inside, and any entry arrangements, can change, so check the official site before you go. If photos are allowed, keep your phone steady and take your time. If they are not, a photo of the outside and the street around it still makes a good record of the visit.
text.geographic_location: In the Kalsa quarter, in the historic centre of Palermo, near the Basilica of Saint Francis of Assisi.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stop is listed for this spot. Make your way to the Kalsa quarter and the Basilica of Saint Francis of Assisi, then look for the oratory nearby. From elsewhere in Palermo, go by taxi or hired scooter and ask to be dropped near the basilica. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the building and for general views of the room. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if the space is tight and you want the whole wall in the frame. Use telephoto (2x to 5x, depending on your phone) to pick out stucco figures and details without leaning in.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. For the exterior, step back and photograph the building from the street nearby. Inside, if photography is allowed, stand near the entrance so you can see the whole room.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the vertical lines straight so walls and doorways do not lean. Take one wide shot, then a few closer ones of single stucco scenes. For the altarpiece, stand square-on and keep the frame level, remembering that it is a replica.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brightest part of a scene to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the stucco keeps its detail. Indoors, hold the phone steady and let night mode work if the phone offers it. Do not use flash, which is often not allowed in churches and oratories.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Check the official site for visiting times, then pick the quietest slot you can for an uncluttered view of the room.

text.access_note: This is a historic oratory that may be ticketed or have restricted hours and photography rules, so check the official site before you go.
